analysis.one_liner: Extends federal protections against racial discrimination in voting for another 25 years.
analysis.headline: The House passed the Voting Rights Act reauthorization 390-33 and the Senate passed it 98-0, and the President signed it into law on July 27, 2006.
analysis.plain_summary: This law renews the core protections of the 1965 Voting Rights Act, which had been set to expire. It keeps federal oversight of states and counties with histories of racial discrimination in voting, requires that voting changes there not weaken minority voters' ability to elect the candidates they prefer, extends bilingual ballots and voting materials through 2032, and allows people who win voting-rights lawsuits to recover expert witness costs. It also replaces federal examiners with federal observers and updates the data used to decide which areas are covered.
analysis.who_benefits: Racial and language minority voters, especially in the states and counties covered by the Act's federal oversight, gain continued protection against voting rules that would dilute their vote. Voters who need ballots and assistance in languages other than English keep that help through 2032. All voters in covered jurisdictions benefit from federal observers monitoring elections.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the Voting Rights Act's core federal oversight provisions for 25 more years, keeping covered jurisdictions from changing election rules without federal approval [S3][S6].

Restores protections narrowed by Supreme Court decisions in Reno v. Bossier Parish II and Georgia v. Ashcroft, stating that any voting rule that diminishes minority voters' ability to elect their preferred candidates denies the right to vote [S3][S6].
Extends the requirement for bilingual election materials through August 5, 2032 [S3][S6].
Lets prevailing parties in voting rights enforcement lawsuits recover expert fees and other reasonable litigation costs, making it easier to bring and sustain such cases [S3][S6].

Directs the Office of Personnel Management to assign federal observers to covered subdivisions where a court authorizes it or the Attorney General finds written evidence that the right to vote is likely to be denied on account of race or color [S3][S6].

analysis.who_pays: State and local election officials in the covered jurisdictions, who must submit proposed voting changes for federal review before implementing them and bear the administrative cost of compliance. Jurisdictions that believe they no longer discriminate can seek release from oversight through a federal court, but Congress chose not to update the coverage formula itself. The federal government also pays for observers and for the bilingual materials mandate's effect on local election budgets.

drawbacks.text: Covered state and local governments bear the cost and delay of clearing every voting change with federal authorities before it takes effect [S3][S6].

Critics in the House offered amendments to weaken the Act, including removing federal oversight and scaling back the bilingual ballot requirement; their objection was that decades-old coverage data no longer reflected conditions in their states. All four amendments were defeated [S8][S9].
Congress chose to keep the existing coverage formula and simply extend it, rather than redesign oversight around current conditions, which covered jurisdictions argued was outdated [S6].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is the continuation of what Congress found, on an extensive legislative record, to be working protections against discrimination in voting; the cost is real but narrow, falling mainly on election administrators in a set of specifically named states and counties. The main honest criticism is that Congress renewed the old coverage formula for 25 years instead of updating it to current conditions, leaving the list of covered jurisdictions fixed. Against that, the bill includes a built-in future reconsideration date and a study of how the bilingual requirements work in practice.

outcome.mechanism: It moved fast and cleared everything: the House passed it 390-33 on July 13, the Senate passed it unchanged 98-0 a week later, and the President signed it into law on July 27, 2006.

narrative.text: Introduced May 2, 2006, the bill cleared the House Judiciary Committee with a 33-1 vote to report it amended within about two weeks [S8].

On July 13, 2006, the House rejected four amendments offered to weaken the bill (from Representatives Norwood, Gohmert, King of Iowa, and Westmoreland) and passed it 390-33; all 197 voting Democrats and the sole Independent voted yes, along with 192 of 230 Republicans [S8][S9].
The Senate took it up by unanimous consent and passed it without amendment on a 98-0 roll call on July 20, 2006 [S8][S10].
The President signed it on July 27, 2006, and it became Public Law 109-246 [S6][S8].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Voters, and especially minority voters in covered jurisdictions, came out ahead: the protections Congress found were still needed were renewed for another 25 years with essentially no opposition in the Senate. Covered state governments, which had sought weaker oversight through floor amendments, did not get the relief they wanted.

sides.party_line_note: The vote was overwhelmingly bipartisan: in the House, all 197 voting Democrats and 192 of 230 Republicans voted yes (390-33), and the Senate passed it 98-0 with no member of either party voting no.

industries.industry: State and local election officials in covered jurisdictions
industries.note: These governments must get federal approval before changing election rules and bear the compliance costs. Their interest in weaker oversight ran against minority voters' interest in continued protection, and their attempts to weaken the bill on the House floor failed.

industries.industry: Voting rights litigators and expert witnesses
industries.note: The law allows prevailing parties in voting rights cases to recover expert fees and other litigation costs, which supports the lawyers and experts who bring discrimination cases on behalf of voters.
